README.html.title: Millia2D Game Engine | millia2d
README.html.summary: Millia2D Game Engine Millia2D is a small game engine framework, focused on providing great APIs to make games focusing on large numbers of entities and agents easier. Key features: easy to use debugging telemetry simple to grasp World Actor Component architecture Throughout the project, I will be looking at implementing various methods of helping create large-scale simulations. My current up-to-date research can be found here. Usage The first step is to create a game class inheriting from MilliaGame, then instantiating your class from wherever you want to use Millia2D. For more tutorials or information, visit the docs or the samples. Installation To install Millia2D, add the latest nuget package to your project: dotnet add package Millia2D License Millia2D is licensed under MIT. See The License for more information. See Third Party Notices for information about dependencies.

For more tutorials or information, visit the docs or the samples. Installation To install Millia2D, add the latest nuget package to your project: dotnet add package Millia2D

report/research/ideas.html.title: Struct clustering | millia2d
report/research/ideas.html.summary: Struct clustering This is similar to Barnes-Hut algorithms https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnes%E2%80%93Hut_simulation If we have loads of entities with the same struct in close enough vicinity, could we create a struct which holds the average values of those for numeric values, and then that be used instead of each individual struct, for the system functionality? eg. for a swarm of ships: position1 position2 position3 position4 position5 Could we only use positionAvg So that the MoveShipSystem only handles the positionAvg, and when later needed, the values get propagated into the real values, and the shift over time from when the clustering started to when the clustering ended is applied individually to each position? If the positionAvg moved (2.3, 1.2), could we then: work out how much each ship moved, based on its own trajectory and how the cluster moved? if position2 was originally moving at (-2.3, -1.2), i.e. the opposite direction what would happen? would this require custom clustering code based on what the struct does? Some questions arise: how would we know when to de-cluster? if these objects move in a cluster and their structs aren't really updated, how would the entity itself know it is being moved? can we temporarily redirect the entity/systems to read the cluster instead of the objects own struct? Data structures Would hashsets work for this? If a big problem of the paradigm is the lookup of which entities have different combinations of components, could we create a hash from the components on an entity, and then use these as a key? Then, to find all relevant entities of a system, all it needs to do is go through the hashset, and go to the specified entry with that hash HashSet<SetItem> set = new(); struct SetItem{ int hash; DataComponent[] components; } points against hashsets: we need "has at least A and B" whereas this provides "has exactly A and B" functionality for querying. hash sets scatter data in memory ECS-like What if instead of revolving the entire engine around ECS, we allow it to be a separate thing, that may be ignored or used as the user pleases. We can still have some sort of entity table which holds references to components, however components may either be Component or DataComponent. Systems will be able to be used to query DataComponents (could it be made to work for normal components as well?) This way, for trivial tasks you can still have a single object handle code and data, whilst for larger stuff you may want to use entities with data components instead. You will also be able to mix and match these. Hopefully.

report/research/issues.html.title: Common issues in game development | millia2d
report/research/issues.html.summary: Common issues in game development These are some common performance issues found in game development, which may give developers performance headaches: object pooling - spawning and deletion of thousands of objects is very costly - we can make an easy API for this even Void Strife has a basic object pooling mechanism, what if this was implemented In-Engine single-threaded loops - most games run like this - can we change this and can we make an easy API for this? rendering - rendering itself will need to be optimized for rendering so many things how can we expose API to users to allow them to influence how groups of entities are rendered, for example batching, other common techniques used pathfinding/AI evaluations

report/research/performance.html.title: Performance metrics | millia2d
report/research/performance.html.summary: Performance metrics A performance target I could aim for is 60fps for ~100,000 actors in the scene. TODO: Try come up with more evaluation metrics/performance targets, especially for things like performance graphs. Evaluation Metrics There is no single evaluation metric which can be created to easily compare game engines. Due to the nature of game engines, a "good" developer may make a game with amazing performance, whilst a "bad" developer may make the same game with much worse performance, but on the same engine. It is easier to compare engines based on the difficulty, or the process, of setting up specific game scenarios and game designs. For instance, with Unity, you have to learn and understand the Unity DOTS package in order to fully take advantage of it, and because it is such a massive subject, that can be quite difficult. Where Millia2D can shine is in the ease of creating a simulation-based game. If the engine is focused and the API is focused to deliver good enough results, it may have a reason of existing. Since the performance of a game in any engine depends on the developers' proficiency with that game engine and hardware, Millia2D should focus on clean, easy to use APIs and less so on raw strength. We can still compare things like frame time or FPS between similar scenarios, but the main target should be to create an engine which is usable and approachable. Entity Component System An ECS will be a data oriented system which acts upon all entities of the same type at once, instead of each entity performing its own calculation. ECS is generally thought of as a composition-over-inheritance pattern. Instead of deeply nested class hierarchies often used in OOP, ECS would provide a data-oriented design, which can provide great benefits to performance, and separation of concerns Unity DOTS Unity DOTS uses the Entity Component System (ECS) design pattern. This is most often used in games, but sometimes used outside of the gaming industry. Inside DOTS, entities and components compose are used for data, and systems for code interacting with that data. From Unity DOTS book An entity is composed of components, where each component is usually C# structs. Components can be added/removed from an entity over its lifetime. Unlike traditional object-oriented patterns in game programming, entities or their components do not usually have their own methods. Instead, each "system" has an update method invoked once per frame, and these updates will read and modify the components of the desired entities. For example, in a monster game, there may be a system called MonsterMoveSystem which modifies the Transform components of every monster entity. Chunks and archetypes In Unity's DOTS, each variation of components on an entity is called an "archetype", and each archetype is stored together in memory. Adding a component to an entity or removing a component from an entity moves the entity to a different archetype. Within an archetype, entities and their components are stored in blocks of memory called chunks. Each chunk stores up to 128 entities, and are stored in their own array in the chunk. ![[Pasted image 20261119223543.png]] The benefit of this system is incredibly fast querying over large numbers of entities. Also, because the arrays are tightly packed, the amount of cache misses decreases greatly, increasing efficiency and the potential ceiling of performance. Caching can also be used to further speed up this process. C# Structs Generally in C#, developers use classes. These are reference types, meaning they hold a reference which points to the actual data somewhere else on the heap. Structs are value types. Instead of holding a pointer to the data, these are the data, and are stored on the stack. The stack offers better cache locality, and overall better performance so structs should generally be used in high-performance scenarios. However, there are certain cases which they aren't the best for. If a struct is quite large in size, copying its values may take some time and thus decrease performance, so it is recommended that structs are kept small and lightweight. Memory A very good target is having components of the same type be contiguous in memory - making iterating through all entities with that component incredibly easy. This is why Unity DOTS's approach below works so well - their table like data structure allows extremely easy querying. Harkonen: "The ideal layout can be achieved by breaking objects into different components, and grouping those components together in the memory by their type. This results in homogenous and sequentially processable data." Multithreading DOD (Data Oriented Design) has a big benefit when it comes to separation of concerns and multithreading. Classically, OOP struggles to take full advantage of multithreading sometimes - differenet components may be using the same data and there may be conflicts, making working on multiple threads much harder. In DOD and ECS especially, it can be a lot easier splitting functionality into different threads. Maybe in the benchmark game, the people simulation is done on one thread, whilst the ship simulation is done on another. Then the master thread combines the result at the end of each frame/simulation tick? Unity DOTS Unity DOTS brings in the C# Job System. From their Unity DOTS book, the C# job system is described with the following: " The job system maintains a pool of worker threads, one for each additional core of the target platform. For example, when Unity runs on eight cores, it creates one main thread and seven worker threads. The worker threads execute units of work called jobs. When a worker thread is idle, it pulls the next available job from the job queue to execute. Once a job starts execution on a worker thread, it runs to completion (in other words, jobs are not preempted). " (page 10) Example code: // A simple example job that multiplies the // elements of two arrays. // Implementing IJob makes this struct a job type. struct MyJob : IJob { // A NativeArray is “unmanaged”, meaning it // isn’t garbage collected. public NativeArray<float> Input; public NativeArray<float> Output; // The Execute method is called when the // job system executes this job. public void Execute() { // Multiply every value in Output by the // corresponding value in the Input array. for (int i = 0; i < Input.Length; i++) { Output[i] *= Input[i]; } } The C# Jobs System is mainly a way for users to perform calculations and processes in a multithreaded way, because generally C# and Unity encourage single-threaded design - that's just what they were made for and that's why they're so easy. Everything gets garbage collected for you. A common downfall when it comes to performance is methods having to be loaded from memory many times, if there is one object type that is spawned a lot in the game. As an example, bullets - these often have classes on each one, and when methods run on each bullet, they have to be loaded from memory. Once we have a couple hundred bullets loaded, a couple hundred methods have had to be loaded, and these bullets are transient, meaning they spawn and despawn and respawn yet again, almost in an endless cycle. One solution to this that is a common fix is object pooling - instead of creating a bullet and then destroying it, we would like to create the bullets at load time, and then re-use them when necessary. If a bullet is no longer used, we can deactivate it and hide it, instead of removing it. This keeps the bullet in memory and removes the need for loading it and its methods from scratch.
